as \mathbf Q-vector spaces. The condition n>1 is used so that the term K_{n-1}(Z) in the localization sequence is a well-defined higher K-group at the position needed; the argument does not otherwise depend on the finiteness of k. \square

lemma_51.statement: Let U be a noetherian scheme, let Z be a regular closed subscheme of U, and let V = U \setminus Z. Let n > 0. If K_n(Z) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} = 0 and K_n(V) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} = 0, then K_n(U) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} = 0.
lemma_51.proof:
Proof. We use the Quillen localization theorem for K-theory of schemes in the standard noetherian form: if U is a noetherian scheme and Z is a regular closed subscheme of U, with V=U\setminus Z, then K(Z)\to K(U)\to K(V) is a homotopy fiber sequence. Equivalently, for every m\ge 0 there is a long exact sequence \cdots\to K_m(Z)\to K_m(U)\to K_m(V)\to K_{m-1}(Z)\to\cdots. The hypotheses of the present lemma are exactly those required for this theorem: U is noetherian by assumption, Z is a regular closed subscheme, and V is the open complement (hence noetherian). Therefore, for the given n>0, the segment K_n(Z)\to K_n(U)\to K_n(V) is exact at K_n(U), i.e. \operatorname{im}(K_n(Z)\to K_n(U))=\ker(K_n(U)\to K_n(V)).

The abelian group \mathbf{Q} is flat over \mathbf{Z}. Indeed, \mathbf{Q}=\mathbf{Z}[1/(\mathbf{Z}\setminus\{0\})] is a filtered colimit of copies of \mathbf{Z}; each copy is free, hence flat, and filtered colimits of flat modules are flat. Consequently, tensoring the exact segment with \mathbf{Q} preserves exactness, so

K_n(Z)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q}\to K_n(U)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q}\to K_n(V)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q}

is exact at the middle term.

By hypothesis, K_n(Z)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q}=0 and K_n(V)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q}=0. Exactness at the middle term then gives

\ker\big(K_n(U)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q}\to 0\big)=\operatorname{im}\big(0\to K_n(U)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q}\big)=0.

But the kernel of the unique map from an abelian group to 0 is the whole group. Hence K_n(U)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q}=0.

The degenerate cases are consistent with the same argument. If Z=\emptyset, then V=U and the hypothesis K_n(V)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q}=0 is exactly the desired conclusion. If V=\emptyset, then Z=U and the hypothesis K_n(Z)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q}=0 is exactly the desired conclusion. If U=\emptyset, all three K-groups are zero. This completes the proof.

lemma_54.statement: Let U be a regular noetherian scheme, let Z be a regular closed subscheme of U, let V=U\setminus Z, and let n>1. Then the sequence K_n(Z)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q} \to K_n(U)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q} \to K_n(V)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q} \to K_{n-1}(Z)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q} induced by the inclusion and restriction maps is exact.
lemma_54.proof: Proof. We use Quillen's localization theorem: if X is a regular noetherian scheme, Z_0 is a regular closed subscheme of X, and W = X \setminus Z_0, then for every integer m \ge 1 there is a long exact sequence of abelian groups \cdots \to K_m(Z_0) \to K_m(X) \to K_m(W) \to K_{m-1}(Z_0) \to K_{m-1}(X) \to \cdots, in which the first map is induced by the closed immersion Z_0 \hookrightarrow X, the second by the open immersion W \hookrightarrow X, and the third is the connecting homomorphism. Apply this theorem with X = U, Z_0 = Z, and W = V. The hypotheses are satisfied exactly as stated: U is regular noetherian by assumption, and Z is a regular closed subscheme of U by assumption. Since n > 1, we have n \ge 2, so the case m = n is allowed. Therefore we obtain an exact sequence K_n(Z) \to K_n(U) \to K_n(V) \to K_{n-1}(Z) \to K_{n-1}(U), with the first map induced by the inclusion Z \hookrightarrow U and the second by the restriction/open immersion V \hookrightarrow U. If Z is empty or equal to U, the same conclusion is immediate from K_*(\varnothing)=0 and the identity map; the theorem also covers these degenerate cases. Next we tensor with \mathbf{Q}. The abelian group \mathbf{Q} is flat over \mathbf{Z}: indeed \mathbf{Q} = S^{-1}\mathbf{Z} with S = \mathbf{Z} \setminus \{0\}, and for any injective homomorphism f:A\to B of \mathbf{Z}-modules, the map S^{-1}f:S^{-1}A\to S^{-1}B is injective, because if s^{-1}a maps to 0, then t f(a)=0 for some t\in S, and injectivity of f gives t a=0, hence s^{-1}a=0. Thus -\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q} is an exact functor on \mathbf{Z}-modules. Applying it to the exact sequence above yields an exact sequence (K_n(Z)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q}) \to (K_n(U)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q}) \to (K_n(V)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q}) \to (K_{n-1}(Z)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q}) \to (K_{n-1}(U)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q}). The maps in this tensored sequence are precisely the original inclusion and restriction maps tensored with the identity on \mathbf{Q}. Exactness of a long exact sequence at its interior terms gives \operatorname{im}(K_n(Z)\otimes\mathbf{Q} \to K_n(U)\otimes\mathbf{Q}) = \ker(K_n(U)\otimes\mathbf{Q} \to K_n(V)\otimes\mathbf{Q}) and \operatorname{im}(K_n(U)\otimes\mathbf{Q} \to K_n(V)\otimes\mathbf{Q}) = \ker(K_n(V)\otimes\mathbf{Q} \to K_{n-1}(Z)\otimes\mathbf{Q}). This is exactly the required exactness of the four-term sequence. No appeal to finite type or to external context is needed; the noetherian hypothesis on U is part of the statement and is used directly in Quillen's theorem. Q.E.D.

lemma_55.statement: Let k be a finite field, let C be a smooth projective curve over k, let p be a closed point of C, and let n > 1. Then K_n(C)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q} is isomorphic to K_n(C\setminus\{p\})\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q} as \mathbf{Q}-vector spaces.
lemma_55.proof:
We prove that K_n(C)⊗_Z Q ≅ K_n(C\{p})⊗_Z Q as Q-vector spaces.

Step 1: Verify the hypotheses of lemma_54.
Let U = C, Z = {p} (viewed as a closed subscheme of C), and V = C \ {p}. We check each condition of lemma_54:

(a) U = C is a regular noetherian scheme. Since C is a smooth projective curve over the finite field k, it is in particular a regular (all local rings are regular local rings) and noetherian (finite type over a noetherian base) scheme.

(b) Z = {p} is a regular closed subscheme of U. The point p is a closed point of the smooth curve C. The local ring O_{C,p} is a discrete valuation ring (regular local ring of dimension 1), and the closed subscheme {p} is defined by the maximal ideal m_p of O_{C,p}. Since O_{C,p}/m_p = κ(p) is a field, the closed subscheme Spec(κ(p)) = {p} is regular (its only local ring is the field κ(p), which is regular of dimension 0).

(c) V = U \ Z = C \ {p} is the open complement.

(d) n > 1 by hypothesis.

All conditions of lemma_54 are satisfied.

Step 2: Identify the K-groups of Z.
The closed subscheme Z = {p} is Spec(κ(p)), where κ(p) is the residue field of p. Since C is a curve over the finite field k and p is a closed point, κ(p) is a finite extension of k, hence κ(p) is itself a finite field.

Step 3: Apply lemma_14 to κ(p).
By lemma_14 (with k replaced by the finite field κ(p)), for every integer m > 0 we have K_m(κ(p))⊗_Z Q = 0.
Since n > 1, we have n ≥ 2 > 0, so K_n(κ(p))⊗_Z Q = 0.
Since n > 1, we have n - 1 ≥ 1 > 0, so K_{n-1}(κ(p))⊗_Z Q = 0.

Step 4: Apply the exact sequence from lemma_54.
By lemma_54, the sequence
K_n(Z)⊗_Z Q → K_n(U)⊗_Z Q → K_n(V)⊗_Z Q → K_{n-1}(Z)⊗_Z Q
is exact, where the maps are induced by the inclusion Z ↪ U and the restriction U → V.
Substituting U = C, Z = Spec(κ(p)), V = C\{p}, and using Step 3, this becomes
0 → K_n(C)⊗_Z Q → K_n(C\{p})⊗_Z Q → 0.

Step 5: Conclude the isomorphism.
From the exactness of the sequence 0 → K_n(C)⊗_Z Q → K_n(C\{p})⊗_Z Q → 0, we deduce:
- The map K_n(C)⊗_Z Q → K_n(C\{p})⊗_Z Q is injective (its kernel is the image of the zero map 0 → K_n(C)⊗_Z Q, which is 0).
- The map K_n(C)⊗_Z Q → K_n(C\{p})⊗_Z Q is surjective (its image is the kernel of the zero map K_n(C\{p})⊗_Z Q → 0, which is all of K_n(C\{p})⊗_Z Q).

Therefore K_n(C)⊗_Z Q ≅ K_n(C\{p})⊗_Z Q as Q-vector spaces, via the restriction map induced by the open immersion C\{p} ↪ C. This completes the proof.
